method_card.title: Averages from Frequency Tables and Grouped Data
method_card.content:
When data are in a frequency table you cannot simply add all values — you must use the frequency-weighted approach.

For an ungrouped frequency table, the mean is \(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}\). The mode is the value with highest frequency. For the median, count through cumulative frequencies to find the \(\frac{\sum f + 1}{2}\)th value.

For a grouped frequency table, individual values are hidden inside class intervals, so you use the midpoint of each class: \(\bar{x} \approx \frac{\sum fm}{\sum f}\). This is always an estimate because using midpoints assumes values are evenly spread within each class.

The modal class has the highest frequency. The median class contains the \(\frac{\sum f}{2}\)th value when counting through cumulative frequencies.
steps: Multiply each midpoint by its frequency: \(fm\)
Sum all \(fm\) values to get \(\sum fm\) and all frequencies to get \(\sum f\)
Identify the modal class (highest frequency) and median class (contains the \(\frac{\sum f}{2}\)th value)
State that the mean is an estimate because midpoints are used

exam_context.marks: 3–5 marks for a full grouped mean; 1–2 marks for modal class or median class identification
exam_context.frequency: One of the highest-frequency calculation topics; appears on nearly every paper

worked_examples.question: Frequency table: value 2 (f=3), value 4 (f=5), value 6 (f=2). Find the mean.
Grouped table: 140–150 cm (f=4), 150–160 (f=9), 160–170 (f=6), 170–180 (f=1). Estimate the mean height.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Estimated mean \(= 3140 \div 20 = 157\) cm. This is an estimate because midpoints represent all values in each class.

worked_examples.question: Grouped table: 0–10 (f=5), 10–20 (f=12), 20–30 (f=8), 30–40 (f=3), 40–50 (f=2). Estimate mean; identify modal class and median class.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Mean = 20 min. Modal class = 10–20 (f=12). Median class = 10–20 (cumulative frequencies 5, 17 — both 15th and 16th values fall here).

Grouped table: 0–10 (f=3), 10–20 (f=8), 20–30 (f=5). What is the modal class?

misconceptions.message: The modal class has the highest frequency. 10–20 has f=8, the highest.

bronze.display: Why is the mean from a grouped table called an estimate?
options: Midpoints are used to represent all values in each class
Grouped data always has measurement errors

misconceptions.message: Individual values within each class are unknown; midpoints assume even spread within the class.

A grouped table has \(\sum fm = 480\) and \(\sum f = 30\). What is the estimated mean?
Frequency table: value 3 (f=1), 5 (f=3), 7 (f=3), 9 (f=1). Total f=8. What is the median? (Find mean of 4th and 5th values.)

misconceptions.message: Cumulative f: 1,4,7,8. 4th value = 5 (end of row 2). 5th value = 7 (start of row 3). Median = (5+7)/2 = 6.

misconceptions.message: \(\sum f=20\). Median between 10th and 11th values. Cumulative f: 3,11. Both values lie in 5–10.

Two groups of 20 students: Group A mean = 55, Group B mean = 65. Combined mean for all 40?
Grouped table: 0–10 (f=4), 10–20 (f=8), 20–30 (f=6), 30–40 (f=2). Midpoints 5,15,25,35. Estimate the mean to 1 d.p.
A student says the modal class is always the best estimate for the mean. Is this correct?
options: Yes, because it has most data points
No, because the mean uses all classes weighted by their midpoints
Yes, if the distribution is symmetric
No, because the mean is always in the first class

misconceptions.message: The mean uses all classes via \(\frac{\sum fm}{\sum f}\). The modal class only identifies the most frequent interval.
